idiom_name: implicit Read[A]/Write[A] derived for a nested case class
implementation_notes: doobie maps column vectors to Scala types with the Read/Write typeclasses: a case class whose elements all have instances gets one derived from its shapeless Generic representation, so a nested case class is simply a value whose fields occupy several positions of the column vector - the pattern's decompose/recompose pair, derived at compile time. The mapper object disappears; what remains is the column order in the query and, for non-case classes, a hand-written Read/Write pair defined in terms of a type that already has instances.
code_sketch:
case class Point(x: Int, y: Int)
case class Vertex(id: Int, start: Point, end: Point)

sql"SELECT id, x1, y1, x2, y2 FROM vertices".query[Vertex]
// Read[Vertex] is derived from the case-class shape: one column per leaf
pitfalls: Derivation works for case classes and tuples, not for arbitrary classes: a value type that is not a case class needs a hand-written Read/Write mapped from a type that is.
The query's column order, not the value type's field names, is what binds the value - swapping x1 and y1 compiles and corrupts the value silently.
Read[Option[A]] maps every column of the value to a nullable type, so an optional embedded value and a value with nullable fields look the same to the typeclass.

variants.name: Slick mapped projection (<>) over the table's columns
variants.idiom_name: Table projection mapped to the case class with the <> operator
variants.implementation_notes: Slick expresses Embedded Value as a mapped projection: the table declares one column per field of the value and the default projection is mapped to the domain case class with the bidirectional <> operator, so the value's fields are ordinary columns of the owner's table and queries can filter on them individually. The classic mapper is replaced by the projection's tupled/unapply pair; the value type stays a plain case class with no persistence knowledge.
pitfalls: The flat projection forces the case class to mirror the columns, so a nested value type needs an extra mapping step - Slick has no composite-value construct of its own.
The <> mapping must be bijective: a lossy unapply silently writes back different values than were read, and Slick only reports it as a runtime mapping error.
Column order in the projection is the mapping, so reordering the tuple while leaving the case class unchanged swaps fields without a compile error.
